title: How Someone Becomes a Saint
description: From martyrs' graves to papal trials, and the saints the calendar later dropped

concepts.title: From Graves to Papal Courts
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of Christian history nobody made a saint by decree. Communities did it themselves. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, written soon after the bishop of Smyrna was burned in the mid second century CE, already describes Christians gathering his bones and meeting each year on the "birthday" of his death. Martyrs' graves became shrines, and holy bishops, monks and ascetics later joined the martyrs. Recognition was local: a bishop approved a cult, usually by elevating or translating the relics to an altar, and the saint's feast entered the local calendar. Peter Brown's The Cult of the Saints (1981) traces how these tombs became centers of late Roman religious and civic life.

The papacy moved in slowly. The first securely documented papal canonization is that of Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, by Pope John XV in 993. Around 1171 to 1172, Pope Alexander III wrote to the king of Sweden objecting to the cult of a man who had been killed while drunk, insisting that no one could be venerated as a saint without the authority of the Roman Church. Historians still debate whether he meant this as a general rule. It became one when an excerpt of the letter, known by its opening word Audivimus, was placed in Pope Gregory IX's law collection, the Liber Extra, in 1234. From then on canonization was, in law, reserved to the pope.

Law and practice diverged for centuries. Popular cults kept springing up around holy men and women, healing wells and wonder-working images, and many never sought or received Rome's approval. The gap between what people venerated and what the Church formally recognized is where most strange saints live.

concepts.title: The Congregation of Rites and the Devil's Advocate
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1588 Pope Sixtus V reorganized the Roman Curia with the bull Immensa Aeterni Dei and created the Sacred Congregation of Rites, a committee of cardinals in charge of both liturgy and saints' causes. Urban VIII tightened the rules: his constitution Caelestis Hierusalem cives (1634) reserved beatification and canonization to the Holy See and forbade public cult of anyone not approved, with an exception for cults that had existed from time immemorial. Prospero Lambertini, made Promoter of the Faith in 1708 and later Pope Benedict XIV, wrote the classic treatise on the procedure (1734 to 1738).

The process was modeled on a trial. Advocates argued for the candidate's heroic virtue or martyrdom and for miracles attributed to them. The Promoter of the Faith (promotor fidei), nicknamed the devil's advocate (advocatus diaboli), raised objections and probed the evidence. The office took shape in the sixteenth century and is first mentioned under Leo X (1513 to 1521).

In 1983 John Paul II's constitution Divinus perfectionis Magister recast the system. The courtroom debate gave way to a historical dossier, the positio, prepared under a relator and judged by historians, theologians and cardinals. The promoter's office survived but lost its prosecuting role, and in practice the number of required miracles fell to one for beatification and one more for canonization; martyrs need none to be beatified. John Paul II went on to canonize about 482 people, more than any pope before him. When the Church took evidence on Mother Teresa in 2003, it heard her critic Christopher Hitchens, whom the press called a devil's advocate, though he held no such office.

concepts.title: Dropped from the Calendar: Christopher and Philomena
concepts.contentHtml:
Being a saint and having a feast on the universal calendar are different things, and confusing them produced a famous myth. In 1969 Paul VI's decree Mysterii Paschalis approved a revised General Roman Calendar. The revisers dropped or localized saints whose stories rested on late legend. Christopher's feast on 25 July left the general calendar because his Acts were judged legendary, and Valentine, Barbara and Catherine of Alexandria were dropped as well. None of them was "de-sainted." Christopher stayed in the Roman Martyrology on 25 July and may still be honored where he is a patron, and Catherine returned to the general calendar in 2002.

The case of Philomena went further. On 24 May 1802 workers in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome found the bones of a young girl behind three tiles reading LUMENA PAXTE CUMFI. Rearranged as PAX TECUM FILUMENA ("peace be with you, Philomena"), the inscription seemed to name an unknown martyr. Her relics went to Mugnano del Cardinale in 1805, a nun's revelations in the 1830s supplied a life story, and cures were reported, including that of the French Catholic organizer Pauline Jaricot in 1835. Jean-Marie Vianney, the Curé of Ars, credited his own reputed miracles to her. In 1837 Gregory XVI authorized a feast on 11 August.

Archaeologists were less sure. Orazio Marucchi argued that the tiles dated from the second century and had been reused on a fourth-century grave, so the name might belong to someone else. On 14 February 1961 the Congregation of Rites ordered her feast removed "from all calendars." Devotion continues at Mugnano, whose supporters cite a 2005 analysis of the tiles in her defense.

title: Saint Guinefort, the Holy Greyhound
description: A dog honored as a martyr near Lyon, the friar who suppressed it, and the historian who traced it

concepts.title: Stephen of Bourbon's Story
concepts.contentHtml:
Our only medieval witness to Saint Guinefort is a hostile one. Stephen of Bourbon (Étienne de Bourbon, died c. 1261) was a Dominican friar who preached and acted as an inquisitor around Lyon. Late in life he compiled a huge, unfinished handbook of moral stories, or exempla, for preachers. In a section on superstition, written in the 1250s, he described what he had found in the diocese of Lyon, near a village of nuns called Neuville, on the lands of the lord of Villars, in the Dombes region north-east of the city.

The local people told him a story. The lord and lady had left their baby in its cradle, guarded by their greyhound, Guinefort. A large snake approached; the dog fought and killed it, and the cradle was overturned in the struggle. Finding the cradle upset and the dog's jaws bloody, the parents and nurse assumed it had killed the child, and the knight drew his sword and killed the dog. Then they found the baby unhurt and the snake dead. Ashamed, they threw the dog into a well, covered it with stones and planted trees around it. Stephen adds that the castle was later destroyed by divine will and the land left deserted.

The peasants, hearing of the dog's loyalty and unjust death, began to visit the place, to honor the dog as a martyr, and to pray to him for sick children. Stephen is precise about places and people because he went there to stamp the practice out. His account shows what a learned preacher saw and condemned, not how the villagers themselves would have described their saint.

concepts.title: The Rite and Schmitt's Reading
concepts.contentHtml:
In the rite Stephen describes, mothers with sick or weak children went to the site, guided by an old woman who taught them the procedure. They offered salt, hung the children's swaddling clothes on the bushes, and passed the naked infants nine times between the trunks of two trees. They called on the fauns of the forest to take back the sick child, which they said belonged to the fauns, and to return their own healthy one. The infant was then left at the foot of the trees beside lit candles; Stephen says some babies were burned to death, and that a wolf nearly took another. Afterward the child was plunged nine times into the nearby river Chalaronne. Stephen had the dog's bones dug up and burned along with the grove, and had the local lords decree that anyone gathering there again would have their goods seized.

The French historian Jean-Claude Schmitt made the case famous in Le saint lévrier (1979), translated as The Holy Greyhound (1983). A historical anthropologist of the Annales school, he read the text against folklore. The tale of a faithful animal wrongly killed after saving a child is international: it appears in the Sanskrit Panchatantra, with a mongoose, in the medieval Seven Sages of Rome, and much later in the Welsh legend of the hound Gelert. The rite, he argued, rested on the changeling belief: a sickly baby was suspected of being a supernatural substitute, and the ordeal aimed to force an exchange.

For the villagers, Schmitt suggested, the cult was neither joke nor heresy: an innocent killed unjustly fitted the pattern of a martyr, and a grave where mothers sought cures fitted that of a healing shrine.

concepts.title: A Cult That Outlived Its Ban
concepts.contentHtml:
Stephen's bonfire did not end the cult. Schmitt combined the thirteenth-century text with later evidence: church records, reports by nineteenth-century clergy and local scholars, place names, and conversations with residents of the Dombes, where he made inquiries from the late 1960s. A wood in the area was still known as the Bois de Saint-Guinefort. The evidence suggests that, despite repeated bans, mothers kept bringing sick children there for centuries; the last known visits date from around the 1930s or 1940s, and older residents still knew the story when Schmitt asked.

Each kind of evidence has its own weakness. Stephen's text is detailed but written by an enemy of the practice, who interpreted the fauns as demons. Later church reports share his hostility. Oral memory recorded in the twentieth century is sympathetic but late, and may have been shaped by the questions asked. Schmitt's method was to let these sources check one another rather than trusting any single one.

The name raises its own puzzle. Guinefort was not invented for the dog: a human saint of that name, associated with Pavia in northern Italy, was honored at churches in France. How the greyhound came to bear a saint's name is unknown, and suggestions that the local cult borrowed it from an existing shrine remain guesses. The Church never recognized the dog, and no pope or bishop approved its cult. Its modern fame owes much to Schmitt's book, and the dog has since reached a wider audience, for instance as the holy greyhound Gwenforte in Adam Gidwitz's children's novel The Inquisitor's Tale (2016).

title: Wilgefortis and the Bearded Virgins
description: A crucified bearded woman, the Lucca crucifix that may explain her, and an English joke about husbands

concepts.title: The Crucified Bearded Woman
concepts.contentHtml:
In churches from Flanders to the Tyrol, visitors still meet a startling image: a crowned woman with a full beard, nailed to a cross and wearing a long gown. She is Wilgefortis, known in Dutch as Ontcommer or Ontkommer, in German as Kümmernis, in English as Uncumber, and in French as Débarras. In Spain and Italy she was often merged with a martyr called Librada or Liberata. The Latin name may come from virgo fortis, "strong virgin," though that is uncertain.

In the commonest version of the legend, she was the Christian daughter of a pagan king of Portugal who had vowed her virginity to God. When her father promised her to a pagan king, in some versions a Moorish one, she prayed to be made repulsive and grew a beard. The suitor withdrew, and her furious father had her crucified, so that she died like the Christ she had chosen as her bridegroom. A popular addition tells of a poor fiddler who played before her image. The statue let fall one of its shoes as a gift; accused of stealing it, he was cleared when the image dropped the second shoe before witnesses. Many images show the fiddler at her feet.

The cult goes back to the fourteenth century. From about 1400 it spread under the name Ontkommer along the Lower Rhine and in the Low Countries, and from about 1470, as Kümmernis, into southern Germany and the Alpine lands, where devotion lasted into the twentieth century. She was entered in the Roman Martyrology in 1583, on 20 July, but was never formally canonized, and the post-Vatican II revision of the martyrology removed her as fictional.

concepts.title: The Volto Santo of Lucca
concepts.contentHtml:
The most widely accepted explanation of the bearded crucified woman points to Lucca in Tuscany. Its cathedral of San Martino houses the Volto Santo ("Holy Face"), a large wooden crucifix of an unusual type. Christ is shown alive, eyes open, bearded and long-haired, wearing a crown and a long belted tunic that reaches to his feet, rather than the loincloth that became standard in the medieval West. Legend said that Nicodemus carved it and that it reached Lucca miraculously in the eighth century. Art historians long dated the surviving figure to the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. Radiocarbon tests announced in 2020 pointed to the late eighth or early ninth century, though critics noted the results had not been peer-reviewed.

The Volto Santo was famous across Europe. The English king William II reportedly swore "by the Holy Face of Lucca," and merchants, pilgrims and confraternities spread painted and carved copies far beyond Tuscany. In 1934 the historians Gustav Schnürer and Josef Ritz argued that northern viewers, used to nearly naked crucified Christs, read these robed, crowned, long-haired figures as a woman, and that a legend grew up to explain what they saw. Lucca also had its own story of a poor minstrel who played before the crucifix and received one of its silver shoes, the same tale later told of Kümmernis.

Later scholars refined the idea rather than abandoning it. Regine Schweizer-Vüllers (1997) treated Kümmernis images as a deliberate borrowing of the Volto Santo type, and Ilse Friesen's The Female Crucifix (2001) explored what a suffering bearded woman meant to her devotees. The Lucca connection explains the image well, but says less about why the cult appealed so strongly to women.

concepts.title: Uncumber, Oats and Thomas More
concepts.contentHtml:
In England the saint became Uncumber, and her specialty became pointed. Women brought her oats in the hope that she would "uncumber" them of their troubles, which in popular telling meant troublesome husbands. Her image stood in Old St Paul's Cathedral in London, and a carved figure of her, bearded and holding a cross, survives among the early sixteenth-century statues of Henry VII's Lady Chapel at Westminster Abbey.

Thomas More recorded the custom in A Dialogue Concerning Heresies (1529), his defense of traditional devotion against Protestant critics. A character called the Messenger, who voices complaints about popular piety, jokes that women have "changed her name" from Wilgefortis to Uncumber "because they reckon that for a peck of oats she will not fail to uncumber them of their husbands." The oats, he guesses, are to provide a horse for an evil husband to ride to the devil on. More's own voice in the dialogue grants that such petitions are superstitious but argues that abuses do not discredit the honoring of saints. Within a decade, the royal injunctions of 1538 ordered the removal of images that drew pilgrimages and offerings, and Uncumber faded from English churches.

Wilgefortis was not the only bearded holy woman. Gregory the Great's Dialogues, from the late sixth century, tell of Galla, a young Roman widow whose doctors warned that unless she remarried she would grow a beard; she chose a convent and accepted the risk. A later Spanish legend from Ávila tells of Paula Barbata, saved from a pursuing suitor when a beard miraculously covered her face. In each story the beard defends a woman's chosen chastity by overturning what the world expected her to look like.

title: Head-Carriers and Dog-Headed Saints
description: Saint Denis and the walking martyrs, and why Eastern icons give Christopher a dog's head

concepts.title: Saint Denis and His Walk
concepts.contentHtml:
The most famous cephalophore (Greek for "head-carrier") is Denis, patron saint of France. The earliest solid witness, Gregory of Tours in the late sixth century, says only that Dionysius was one of several bishops sent to Gaul, became bishop of Paris, and was beheaded with a sword. Historians place his death in the third century, probably in the persecution under Decius shortly after 250 CE. Early medieval legend added companions, Rusticus and Eleutherius, and the miracle that made him famous: the beheaded body rose and carried its head to the place where he wished to be buried.

The legend grew in the ninth century. In 827 the Byzantine emperor Michael II sent Louis the Pious a manuscript of mystical treatises attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian converted by Paul in Acts 17:34. Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, had them translated and in the 830s wrote a new Passion identifying the Paris martyr with both the Areopagite and the treatises' author. His Denis walks from Montmartre, head in hands and escorted by singing angels, to the site of the future abbey. The Golden Legend spread this version across Europe. Told how far the saint had walked, the eighteenth-century hostess Madame du Deffand reputedly replied that only the first step is difficult.

Peter Abelard, then a monk of Saint-Denis, questioned the identification around 1121 and had to flee the abbey. Scholars now separate three men: the first-century Areopagite, the third-century bishop of Paris, and an anonymous Syrian writer of about 500 CE known as Pseudo-Dionysius. Even the reading of Montmartre as mons martyrum, "mount of the martyr," is uncertain; it may come from a hill of Mercury or Mars.

concepts.title: A Hundred Headless Walkers
concepts.contentHtml:
Denis had many counterparts. The French scholar Marcel Hébert first used the term "cephalophore" in 1914, and the folklorist Émile Nourry, writing as Pierre Saintyves, counted 134 cases in French hagiography alone. Examples cluster in France but reach across Europe:

  • Nicasius, bishop of Reims, killed by invaders in the early fifth century, finished his verse of Psalm 119 after his head was struck off.
  • Felix and Regula, patrons of Zürich, were said to have walked forty paces uphill with their heads before lying down; the Grossmünster stands over their supposed graves.
  • Minias of Florence carried his head to the hillside where San Miniato al Monte now stands.
  • Osyth, an Anglo-Saxon abbess in Essex, walked with her head to a convent door.
  • Valerie of Limoges brought her head to her teacher, Saint Martial.

Several explanations for the motif are offered, and they can overlap. One is iconographic: artists showed beheaded martyrs holding their heads as an emblem of how they died, as Catherine holds her wheel, and viewers and storytellers may have read the emblem literally. Another is practical: in a world of relic thefts and rival shrines, a saint who walked to a spot and lay down there had personally chosen his resting place, which strengthened a church's claim to the body. A third is literary: John Chrysostom pictured martyrs presenting their severed heads to Christ, like soldiers showing their wounds to a king. Some modern writers link the stories to a pre-Christian Celtic cult of heads, but that idea rests on thin evidence and remains speculative.

concepts.title: Christopher the Dog-Head
concepts.contentHtml:
In the West, Christopher is the giant ferryman of the Golden Legend (c. 1260): a Canaanite named Reprobus who resolved to serve the greatest master, carried a child across a river, found the child as heavy as the world, and learned he had borne Christ, hence his name, "Christ-bearer." A popular belief held that whoever saw his image would be safe from sudden death that day, hence the huge Christophers painted opposite church doors. Many Orthodox icons show him differently, as a warrior saint with the head of a dog.

The icons follow the oldest texts. The Greek Passion of Christopher, dated to the fifth century or later, makes him a cynocephalus (dog-head) named Reprebos, from a tribe of cannibals, mute until he prays and is given speech, then baptized and martyred under Decius. A Coptic text about the apostle Bartholomew features a similar dog-headed cannibal converted with an angel's help. In the 980s the Latin poet Walter of Speyer still described Christopher as a giant of a dog-headed race in the land of the Canaanites, who ate human flesh and barked.

Greek and Roman writers from Ctesias to Pliny placed dog-headed peoples at the edges of the known world, and Christian thinkers from Augustine to the ninth-century monk Ratramnus of Corbie asked whether such beings descended from Adam and could be saved. A converted dog-head was the ultimate outsider brought in, proof of baptism's power. Some scholars also suspect a confusion between Latin Cananeus, "Canaanite," and canineus, "doglike," though they disagree about which way it ran. Russian painters made dog-headed Christophers from the later sixteenth century until a church synod banned the image in 1722; Old Believers kept painting them.

title: Holy Fools
description: Byzantine saloi, Russian yurodivye, and why anyone would seek holiness by seeming mad

concepts.title: The Byzantine Salos
concepts.contentHtml:
Paul told the Corinthians that "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing" and called himself and his fellow apostles "fools for Christ's sake" (1 Corinthians 1:18 and 4:10). A small number of Christians took the phrase literally. The Greek word for them was salos, roughly "crazy." An early example appears in Palladius's Lausiac History (c. 420): a nun at an Egyptian convent of the Tabennesi, later named Isidora in tradition, who feigned madness, did the dirtiest work and was mocked by the other sisters until a visiting holy man revealed her as the holiest of them all. She then fled to escape their reverence.

The classic figure is Symeon of Emesa (modern Homs in Syria), who lived in the sixth century. The church historian Evagrius Scholasticus, writing in the 590s, mentions him, but most of what we know comes from a Life by Leontius, bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus, written in the mid seventh century. Leontius says Symeon spent about 29 years as a desert ascetic near the Dead Sea with his companion John, then entered Emesa dragging a dead dog behind him. In church he put out the lamps and threw nuts at the women; he ran into the women's baths and flouted fasts in public. In secret he cured the sick, helped the poor and foresaw disasters.

Leontius's Life is hagiography with a purpose, and scholars such as Derek Krueger read it as a portrait of the late antique city as much as a biography. A later Life of Andrew the Fool, set in fifth-century Constantinople but probably written in the tenth, is generally regarded as a literary creation rather than the record of a real person.

concepts.title: Russia's Yurodivye and Saint Basil's
concepts.contentHtml:
The holy fool found a second home in Russia, where he was called yurodivy. The Life of Andrew the Fool was translated into Slavonic and shaped Russian expectations. It also supplied the vision behind the feast of the Pokrov, the Intercession of the Mother of God, in which Andrew sees Mary spread her veil over worshippers in Constantinople's Blachernae church. The first Russian fool to be canonized was Procopius of Ustyug (died 1303), and the Russian Orthodox Church now counts 36 yurodivye among its saints.

The most famous is Basil the Blessed (Vasily Blazhenny), born near Moscow about 1468, died in 1552 or 1557 (sources disagree). He went naked through Moscow winters, wore iron chains, and was remembered for rebuking Ivan the Terrible for letting his mind wander during the liturgy. Later tradition adds that he stole from merchants for the poor, and stoned the houses of the pious, where demons lurked outside, while kissing sinners' walls, where angels wept. He was canonized in 1588. In 1570, during Ivan's assault on Novgorod and Pskov, Nicholas of Pskov reportedly confronted the tsar; Pskov tradition says he offered Ivan raw meat in Lent, and the city was largely spared.

The many-domed church on Red Square, built in 1555 to 1561 to celebrate Ivan's capture of Kazan in 1552, is officially the Cathedral of the Intercession on the Moat. Basil was buried beside it, and in 1588 a chapel was added over his grave; his name replaced the official one in everyday use. Most historians regard the story that Ivan blinded the architects so they could never build anything finer as a myth; the builder appears in later records at work elsewhere.

concepts.title: The Logic of Holy Folly
concepts.contentHtml:
Seeking holiness by seeming mad looks perverse, but writers inside the tradition gave several connected reasons. The first is humility. Monks feared vainglory, the pride that feeds on a reputation for holiness, and a saint taken for a lunatic is never admired; Isidora fled once found out. The second is prophetic freedom. A man thought mad can tell the powerful what no courtier dares. The English envoy Giles Fletcher, in Of the Russe Commonwealth (1591), described naked fools in Moscow's streets and noted that people let them speak freely even against the great. The third is exposure: by breaking rules in public, the fool shows up the hypocrisy of respectable piety, echoing Christ, himself mocked before the crucifixion.

The tradition had a built-in problem. Holy folly cannot be verified from outside, since the same behavior may be sanctity, illness or fraud, and the audience must decide which. Sergey Ivanov, in Holy Fools in Byzantium and Beyond (2006), stresses that the holy fool needs onlookers, whose shock is part of the act. Church authorities stayed wary. The Council in Trullo (692) ordered penalties for people who feigned demonic possession, a canon often read as aimed partly at would-be fools, and Peter the Great's church reforms in the eighteenth century treated many wandering fools as impostors.

The figure survived regardless. Xenia of St Petersburg, widowed young in the eighteenth century, gave away her property, wore her dead husband's clothes, answered only to his name and wandered the city; the Russian Orthodox Church canonized her in 1988. In literature, the yurodivy of Pushkin's Boris Godunov tells the tsar to his face that no one may pray for a Herod.

title: Saints Who Never Were
description: A Christianized Buddha, saints made from words, and Mexico's unofficial folk saints

concepts.title: Josaphat, the Buddha in Disguise
concepts.contentHtml:
For centuries Christians honored a saint whose story was the life of the Buddha. The tale of Barlaam and Josaphat tells of an Indian king who, warned that his son will adopt the religion he persecutes, shuts the prince away from every sight of suffering. The prince, Josaphat, nevertheless encounters disease, disability and old age, learns that everyone dies, and is converted by the hermit Barlaam, later renouncing his throne to live as an ascetic. The parallels to the Buddha's sheltered youth, his encounters with age, sickness and death, and his renunciation are unmistakable.

A Buddhist account of the prince's life passed, probably through Manichaean versions in Central Asia, into Arabic as the Kitab Bilawhar wa-Budasaf, current in eighth-century Baghdad. A Christian Georgian version, the Balavariani, followed by about the tenth century, and the Georgian monk Euthymius of Athos (died 1028) is now generally credited with the Greek text long attributed to John of Damascus. A Latin translation appeared in 1048, and from there the Golden Legend and dozens of vernaculars. The name tracks the route: Sanskrit bodhisattva became Arabic Budasaf, then Yudasaf through a misplaced dot in Arabic script, Greek Ioasaph and Latin Josaphat.

Barlaam and Josaphat entered the church calendars: the Greek church commemorates them on 26 August, and older editions of the Roman Martyrology listed them on 27 November. Marco Polo, describing Sri Lanka around 1300, wrote that had the Buddha been a Christian he would have been a great saint, without seeing the link to Josaphat. The Portuguese historian Diogo do Couto noticed the resemblance around 1600, and Édouard Laboulaye and Felix Liebrecht established it in 1859 and 1860.

concepts.title: Expedite and Other Saints Made of Words
concepts.contentHtml:
Some saints owe their existence to a slip of the pen. Expeditus appears in the Hieronymian Martyrology, an early calendar of martyrs, in a group said to have died at Melitene (now Malatya in Turkey) on 19 April. The Bollandist Hippolyte Delehaye argued in the early twentieth century that the name was probably a copyist's misreading of another, such as Elpidius. Whatever its origin, the name (Latin expeditus, "prompt") made Expedite the saint of urgent causes.

A popular story, told in Paris and in New Orleans, says a case of relics or a statue arrived marked expédit or "expedite," and the recipients mistook the shipping instruction for a name. The tale is folklore, since the name is far older, but it is now part of the cult. Images show a Roman soldier crushing a crow whose banner reads cras ("tomorrow," which also imitates a crow's call) while he holds up a cross marked hodie ("today"): conversion, and help, should not be put off. Rome tried to discourage the cult in the early 1900s, with little effect. Expedite is patron of Acireale in Sicily, draws huge crowds in São Paulo, and red roadside shrines dot the island of Réunion.

Other saints may have been made the same way. Bede tells how the British martyr Alban sheltered a fleeing priest and put on his cloak; in Geoffrey of Monmouth's twelfth-century history the priest becomes Amphibalus, a Latin word for a cloak, and a cult of Saint Amphibalus followed at St Albans. The name of Veronica, whose veil bore Christ's face, is often explained as vera icon, "true image," though many scholars prefer Berenice, the name the apocryphal Acts of Pilate give the woman Jesus healed of bleeding.

concepts.title: Mexico's Folk Saints: Santa Muerte and Malverde
concepts.contentHtml:
Folk saints are figures venerated as saints without official recognition, and sometimes against it. Latin America has many, such as Argentina's Difunta Correa; two Mexican figures have caused the most alarm. Santa Muerte ("Holy Death") is death personified as a robed female skeleton with a scythe and a globe. Devotees light candles in colors matched to their petitions, such as red for love and gold for money. Eighteenth-century Inquisition records describe Indigenous Mexicans venerating a skeletal figure, but the open public cult is recent. In 2001 Enriqueta Romero put a life-size statue on display at her home in Tepito, a working-class Mexico City neighborhood, and the shrine became a center of devotion.

The scholar R. Andrew Chesnut estimated in 2012 that she had perhaps 10 to 12 million followers, mostly in Mexico and the United States, a figure hard to check. Many devotees are young, urban and working-class, and many are women. She is popular in prisons and among people who feel unprotected by the state, including some traffickers, which feeds a lurid image that scholars say misrepresents most followers. Catholic leaders have condemned the devotion; in 2013 Cardinal Gianfranco Ravasi, a senior Vatican official, called it blasphemous.

Jesús Malverde, the "angel of the poor" of Culiacán in Sinaloa, is honored as a bandit who robbed the rich for the poor and was killed by the authorities, traditionally on 3 May 1909, now his feast day. No contemporary record of him has been found, and the journalist Sam Quinones suggests the legend blends two documented Sinaloan bandits, Heraclio Bernal and Felipe Bachomo. His chapel in Culiacán draws migrants, the sick and the poor as well as traffickers, whose devotion earned him the nickname "narco-saint."
